ami_style_notes: Turns shift from short, informal exchanges to long, structured speaker monologues, then back to medium-length questions and answers. Overlap is light but frequent backchannels—“yeah,” “okay,” and brief acknowledgments—keep the pace conversational. Speakers use fillers, repetitions, false starts, and mid-sentence repairs; uncertainty comes through in phrases such as “I think,” “maybe,” and “it seems.” Questions are often softened with a compliment or framed as curiosity, and answers build on them while acknowledging what remains unclear. Challenges are indirect and collegial rather than confrontational.
research_problem: Which neighborhood rain gardens to select for a joint flood resilience field study

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Four years studying urban stormwater with rain gauges and sensors that measure flow into and out of rain gardens. She led the preliminary storm-by-storm comparisons and checks whether the readings are reliable across different rainfall conditions.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She treats measured runoff reduction as evidence about what happens at a garden, not necessarily what happens on nearby streets. She wants to know whether the observed storms are representative and whether water bypassed the sensors. She is wary of using drainage access or reports of disruption as substitutes for measured water movement, while welcoming those findings as separate pieces of the study.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Professor Luis Ortega
speakers.background: Fifteen years designing and evaluating municipal drainage retrofits. He has reviewed as-built plans, traced inlet and outlet connections on site, and assessed safe access for installing and maintaining flow monitors before storm season.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He focuses on whether each site has a legible drainage area, workable instrument locations, and a maintenance setup that will keep the field data usable. He knows a clean installation does not establish downstream flood benefit, and is unsure how far conventional hydraulic checks can resolve the neighborhood-scale question. He invites the others to identify what his site inspections might miss.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Amina Okafor
speakers.background: Five years evaluating neighborhood infrastructure projects using resident surveys, business interruption records, and comparisons between similar blocks. She is developing measures of flood-related travel delays, missed work, and property disruption for the next study stage.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She asks whether changes in water flow could plausibly translate into disruptions people experience, and whether those disruptions can be compared fairly across the selected neighborhoods. She is skeptical that strong garden measurements or convenient monitoring alone indicate a meaningful resilience benefit; exposure, reporting differences, and other drainage improvements may also shape the results. She wants to build those concerns into a feasible field plan with the team.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: In the meeting dialogue, have the hydrologist use preliminary inflow-and-outflow runoff measurements to support selecting the Willow Street and Maple Avenue rain gardens. Have the civil engineer discuss whether those sites can be monitored, and the environmental economist keep the broader goal of understanding neighborhood flood disruption in view. The team should make the shared site-selection decision during the meeting. Let one premise emerge implicitly: that stronger measured runoff reduction at these gardens is a useful indicator of their contribution to neighborhood flood resilience under the storms the study aims to understand. Participants may question how the measurement serves the broader goal, but should not explicitly name or flag this premise as an assumption.

ground_truth.assumption: The gardens' relative performance on measured runoff reduction is a useful indicator of their relative contribution to neighborhood flood resilience under the storms of interest.
ground_truth.dependent_decision: Select the Willow Street and Maple Avenue rain gardens as the pair for the next field-study stage because their preliminary runoff measurements show stronger reduction than those of the other eligible sites.
ground_truth.disciplinary_context: Hydrology supplies event-based inflow-and-outflow measurements; civil engineering establishes that the sites and their drainage connections can be monitored; environmental economics frames the broader outcome as flood-related disruption to the surrounding neighborhood.
ground_truth.why_needed: The team is using a garden-level hydrology measurement to choose sites for a study of broader neighborhood flood resilience. That choice depends on the measurement being informative about the broader goal.
ground_truth.risk_if_false: If measured runoff reduction does not indicate a garden's contribution to neighborhood flood resilience under the storms of interest, the selected pair could perform well on the monitored measure without meaningfully reducing nearby flood disruption, limiting what the field study can conclude about resilience.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Thanks for squeezing into the lab room. With equipment due May 22, I’d like us to leave with two sites the crew can actually instrument.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Right. Willow and Maple are both strong on the storms we measured; I’d like to check the heavier events for gaps before we lock them in.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: That’d help. For those heavier storms, could we check whether the nearby blocks had street closures? I’d like to know whether the strong garden measurements line up with disruptions people actually experienced.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, I can match the heavier storms in the gauge file to closure dates. Amina, could you check whether those closures were on the blocks draining toward Willow and Maple, rather than just nearby?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, I can map those closure locations against Luis’s drainage connections. The closure records may not show which direction the water came from, though.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Right, my survey traces the pipe connections, not where water moves across the street when it ponds. If you send me the closure locations, I can check them against the inlet elevations and low points.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That would help. While you’re looking at the low points, could you flag any route where water might have gone around our inlet sensors during the heavier storms? That could change how I read those reductions.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Yeah, I’ll check the parallel catch basins upstream of each sensor. If they start taking flow in heavier storms, our measured inlet volume may not represent the same drainage area.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: If those parallel basins take flow, could you mark which blocks they serve? That’d help me pick comparison blocks with similar flood exposure, not just nearby streets.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Yeah, I can mark the tributary blocks for those basins. Some curb inlets sit right at drainage-area boundaries, though, so I’ll flag those rather than draw a hard line.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Okay, the flagged boundary blocks can stay out of the comparison for now. I can use the 311 calls to find places to ask residents and businesses about missed work or closures, rather than treating call counts as the disruption measure.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Yeah, those conversations might also tell us where to check for recurring inlet clogging. A monitor can keep logging while a grate fills with debris, and then we’re measuring a maintenance problem as much as the garden.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, do your site notes say whether either grate was clogged during our monitored storms? I can flag those events in the storm comparison.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Not event by event, no—I inspected after those storms. I’ll check the crew photos for debris at either grate, but I wouldn’t flag a storm as clogged from my notes alone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I won’t mark any storm as clogged without dated evidence. I’ll also check the gauge file for larger storms we missed entirely at Willow or Maple, so we know what conditions those reductions actually cover.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Could you send me the dates of those missed storms? I’ll check whether other drainage work was underway near Willow or Maple then, so we know what residents might be remembering.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Sure, I’ll send the missed-storm dates, with the gauge totals so you can see how big they were. That might help separate drainage work from storm conditions.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Great, the totals will help me pick a couple of comparable storms to ask residents and businesses about, rather than just asking whether they’ve had flooding.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: When you ask about those storms, could you distinguish street ponding from basement sewer backups? Those may be different hydraulic pathways, and my connection survey wouldn’t tell us which residents experienced.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, I’ll ask about those separately. For street ponding, I’ll also ask whether it blocked someone’s usual route to work—that gets us closer to the disruption we’re trying to measure.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: For those route questions, I can send the storm times, not just dates. Whether the street was blocked during the morning commute or later might matter.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, please send the times. I can ask about trips people actually made during those hours, including evening shifts, rather than assuming everyone commutes in the morning.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Right, I’ll send the start and end times too, so you can match trips to the storm.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: I think we should confirm Willow and Maple for the May 22 reservation; the crew can install and service monitors at both. If the closure mapping shows we’re looking at different drainage paths, though, let’s catch that before installation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Okay, let’s reserve Willow and Maple. I’ll map the closures against your low points before installation and flag it quickly if either garden doesn’t connect to the blocks where people were disrupted.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I’ll send the storm times and missed-event dates tomorrow. If the heavier-storm checks change how I read either site, I’ll flag it before installation.

The dialogue does not establish that the two gardens outperform other eligible sites.

transcript.text: Sorry about the room shuffle. I’d like us to leave with two sites today, so we can get the monitors ordered before storm season.

transcript.text: Yeah, could we put the drainage maps beside the storm log? I’d like to see whether overflow from either garden reaches the streets where those service requests came from.

transcript.text: Yeah, I’ve got the connection sketches here. We can trace Willow and Maple from the outlets toward the street inlets, though I’d want to verify the overflow path on site.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: That site check would help. Could we note which homes, shops, or usual travel routes sit along each overflow path? Then I can plan where to ask about disruption.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Yeah, I can put the street grades and curb inlets on these sketches. That should help narrow down which frontages and walking routes to ask about, rather than treating the whole block alike.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Great. I can use the service requests to pick frontages to visit, but I wouldn’t use request counts to rank Willow against Maple—Southbank and Mill Ward may report flooding differently.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Right, and before we lean too hard on the Willow–Maple readings, I want to check whether both held up across light and heavy storms, not just one good event.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Maya, if the heavy-storm readings look odd, flag the events for me. I can check whether sediment or debris shifted the inlet flow away from the monitor.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Great, I’ll send you the heavy-storm events that need a closer look.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: While you’re checking those events, Luis, could we ask Public Works whether either block has had other drainage work recently? I’d hate to attribute fewer flooded trips to a garden when a new inlet helped too.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Yeah, I’ll ask Public Works for the work orders on both blocks—especially inlet replacements or pipe cleaning since the storm log started.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Great, those work orders will help me decide which nearby streets make sense to compare.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Mm, Willow and Maple both have safe monitor access, so I can put them on a regular pre-storm check route. That should keep the data usable while we sort out the comparison streets.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, with that access in place, I’m comfortable choosing Willow and Maple for monitoring. They’re promising places to test the neighborhood question, not sites where we’ve already shown less street flooding.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: I’m comfortable with Willow and Maple as the pair. Could I do a few short conversations on both blocks before summer storms, so we know what travel or work disruptions to watch for?

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Yeah, do those conversations before we install anything; I can walk the overflow routes with you and flag where the grades suggest water actually crosses a travel path.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Great, I’ll bring a short set of questions for that walk.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Great. While we’re walking, I can mark a couple of repeatable photo points at the low crossings. That might help us check what happens there after a storm.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Could we timestamp those photos against the monitor readings? I’d like to see whether water at the crossings shows up during the same part of the storm as the garden overflow.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Yeah, I can timestamp them and mark the photo bearings. We’ll need someone there during the storm, though; the post-storm shots won’t tell us when the crossing flooded.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Could we ask a couple of nearby shops to text us when a crossing becomes hard to use? If they’re willing, that might give us a rough time even when none of us can be there.

transcript.speaker: Professor Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Yeah, if the shops are willing, let’s ask them to include which crossing and the time in the text, so Maya can line it up with the logger. I’ll put Willow and Maple on the site list.

run_config.research_problem: Which neighborhood rain gardens to select for a joint flood resilience field study
run_config.benchmark_task: Generate one implicit, decision-dependent premise: the team uses a hydrology measurement such as infiltration or runoff reduction to choose a pair of rain garden sites for a broader flood resilience study. The shared site-selection decision must be made during the meeting, drawing on the method and broader goal. The premise connecting the measure to that goal should be inferable from actual dialogue but left unspoken. Ground truth should focus on the measurement-based choice, without arbitrary counts of the total candidate pool or numerical cutoffs. Include a conditional risk if the premise were false.
